chapter_theme: The second half of Kapilar's Kurinjikkali (52 to 65): the friend pressing a night visitor to marry, the girl recounting the lover's wooing and the night tryst, a run of kaikkilai addresses by a man to a girl too young to answer (56 to 59), and comic dialogues in which the suitor, the friend and the girl argue over grace, debt, virtue and the palm-stem horse.

52.reading: The friend tells the hill lord, whose tusker has killed the tiger that leapt at it and walks among its herd, that when he comes by night to her trysts the hamlet takes him by his lotus chaplet for the mountain goddess, the millet watchers with torches, slings and bows shout that he is an elephant, and the town hears him as a tiger on the pepper slopes; if they ever find the man instead of the beast she will not live, nor will the friend, so let him come at dawn, ask for her and marry her, and the friend will watch his new look and her bride's shyness.
52.nuance: The three refrains pair his three night-costumes (lotus chaplet and sandal, wet cloth and evening garland, the chest with its necklace) with three misreadings, goddess, elephant, tiger, so the danger is spelled out as the one mistake not yet made: the true one. The opening tusker likened to Bhima breaking the thigh of the leader of the hundred and to Mal among the wrestlers is the lover's strength that the dawn proposal asks him to use openly; it has no second pair of correspondences, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet watch, hill slopes and the night tryst of kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the tusker goring the tiger, like the one who broke the thigh of the hundred's leader
the victorious tusker among its herd, like Mal who felled the wrestlers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend turns away the night visits and asks him to come at dawn and marry (வதுவை அயர்தல் வேண்டுவல்)

iraicchi.act: the tusker stays beside his loving she-elephant after fighting off a rival
iraicchi.sense: even the beast on his hill keeps by its mate, while the hero has taken the girl and left her

53.reading: The friend tells the lord of the rain-fed hill, where a tusker stays beside his loving cow after wounding a rival and kaanthal buds open like its tusks, that after he took the girl in secret and then left her she might have borne the slipping bangles, the neighbours' talk and the heart's sorrow, had her eyes not run like water spat by carp, her brow not paled like the peerkku flower, and her nights not been broken by dreams; and that, as the drying millet on his hill revives when rain falls, her beauty will revive with his grace.
53.nuance: Each refrain grants a loss that could be endured and then names the sign that cannot be hidden from the town (tears, pallor, sleeplessness), so the argument for marriage is built from what gossip can see. The closing millet simile takes the hill's own crop for the girl, so the plea to marry is put in the hero's own landscape.

thinai_evidence.note: elephant, kaanthal and millet of the rainy hill

comparisons.tenor: kaanthal buds rising like the tusks that wounded the rival
her tears like water spat out by carp
her pallid brow taking the colour of the peerkku flower
her beauty reviving at his grace as dried millet revives with rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend tells the hero of the girl's suffering since he withdrew and asks for his grace (நின் அளி பெற நந்தும்)

54.reading: The girl tells her friend how her lover, asking whether it was fitting that she would not grant grace to one who served at her feet, took her fragrant hair and smelled the braid, laid her fingers over his eyes and sighed like a bird that cannot fly, and stroked her painted breast as a love-mad tusker soothes his cow; he has taken away her distress, so if the friend will speak so that the house's guard is not broken, she will plan it with her, that it may be said she did this out of love, which in an unlasting world is the thing that lasts.
54.nuance: The heroine borrows the puram formula for fame in a world that does not last (மன்னா உலகத்து மன்னுவது) for a woman's choice of her lover: the thing she wants remembered is that she acted from love. Lines 16 and 17 (நம் நகர் அரும் கடி நீவாமை கூறின்) are compressed, and whether she means disclosure to the family is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers' union in kalavu and the move toward disclosure

comparisons.vehicle: நறாஅ அவிழ்ந்தன்ன என் மெல் விரல் போது
comparisons.tenor: her soft fingers like opening honey-flowers
his sigh like a bird that cannot fly
his caress like a love-mad tusker soothing its cow

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl recounts the union and asks the friend to help so the love is not hidden

55.reading: The girl tells her friend that he stopped her, looked at her brow, face, shoulders, eyes, gait and speech, and said each was not a crescent for it does not wane, not the moon for it has no stain, not a hill though bamboo crowds it, not a pool though flowers crowd it, not a peacock though it moves softly, not a parrot though it falters; then, praising her, he watched his moment like a netter and looked pitifully like a beggar, bowed and touched her, he who is like a tusker no post can hold, and his nature, friend, is not a simple man's.
55.nuance: The six denials are the hero's praise in the form of corrected similes: each standard vehicle is named and refused for a flaw it has and she lacks, so the praise works by finding fault with the moon. The netter and the pulaiyar similes let the girl see the calculation in his humility, which is why she ends by saying he is no simpleton.

thinai_evidence.note: the first meeting and the lover's approach in kalavu

comparisons.vehicle: மின் ஒளிர் அவிர் அறல் இடை போழும் பெயலே போல்
comparisons.tenor: the shining parting of her dark hair, like lightning splitting the rain
her brow, which does not wane as the crescent does
her face, stainless unlike the moon
her soft gait, like and unlike the peacock's
her faltering speech, like and unlike the parrot's
he watched for her unguarded moment as netters do
his pitiful look like a beggar's

comparisons.vehicle: காழ் வரை நில்லாக் கடும் களிறு அன்னோன்
comparisons.tenor: the lover, strong as a tusker no post can hold

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl tells her friend how the man stopped and praised her; the opening vocative (நல் நுதால்) is read as addressed to the friend

56.reading: The man, seeing a girl come with ngaazhal clusters in her hair and a face like the moon, asks whether she is a doll a craftsman made, a woman built from all good women's parts, or Death in a form it chose, says her people are wrong to leave her unguarded, and tells her that her beauty like swan, peahen and dove bewilders those who see her, her shoulders like bamboo, pillow and raft torment them, and her young breasts take their lives; then, as she passes without a word, he says neither she nor her people are at fault, only the king, who does not have a drum beaten before her as before a killer elephant let out to water.
56.nuance: The girl is too young to know what she does (பேதுற்றாய்ப் போல... நீ அறியாய்), so the address is one-sided, the kaikkilai of porul 1.53. The closing conceit turns the blame into a civic complaint: she is a public danger the king should announce by drum like a must elephant.

thinai_evidence.note: his love is spoken to a girl too young to answer it

comparisons.vehicle: அகல் மதி தீம் கதிர் விட்டது போல
comparisons.tenor: her smiling face like the broad moon sending out sweet rays

comparisons.vehicle: அனம் என, அணி மயில் பெடை எனத், தூது உண் அம் புறவு என
comparisons.tenor: her beauty like the swan, the peahen and the dove

comparisons.vehicle: அமைத் திரள் என, நுண் இழை அணை என, முழங்கு நீர்ப் புணை என
comparisons.tenor: her shoulders like bamboo, a soft pillow and a raft in the roaring flood

comparisons.vehicle: கோங்கின் முகை என, முகம் செய்த குரும்பை எனப், பெயல் துளி முகிழ் என
comparisons.tenor: her young breasts like the kongu bud, the coconut bud and the rain-drop bud

comparisons.vehicle: நிறை அழி கொல் யானை நீர்க்கு விட்டாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the girl let out unannounced, like a killer elephant sent to water

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man first speaks to himself (lines 1 to 13), then to the girl, who does not answer

57.reading: The man tells the girl who ran past from her father's old house with her ball, her waist so slight it could not be told from creeper, lightning or goddess, that with eyes finer than the blue lily of the Pandya's Koodal she has reddened him like that king's spear against hostile elephants, that she wounds worse than his arrows that pierce enemies' breasts, and that her breasts are fiercer than his elephant's tusks, asking whether this is fitting; at that she bowed, looked at the ground, glanced sharply at her companions and went home, taking his wits with her.
57.nuance: Each praise runs through the Pandya's war gear (spear, arrows, tusked elephant), so the girl's harm is measured against a king's violence and found greater. Her silent going, eyes lowered and then flashing at her friends, is the first sign of a response, but the address remains his alone.

thinai_evidence.note: praise addressed to a young girl at play who goes without answering

comparisons.tenor: her rounded shoulders like bamboo

comparisons.vehicle: கொடி என, மின் என, அணங்கு என
comparisons.tenor: her slight waist like a creeper, lightning, a goddess

comparisons.vehicle: அவிழ் நீலத்து அலர் வென்ற அமர் உண் கண்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes surpassing the opening blue lily of Koodal
her reddening wound on him beyond the Pandya's spear on enemy elephants
her skin like the tender leaf of the young mango
her golden spots like young vengai blossom
her breasts fiercer than the tusks of the Pandya's elephant

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man addresses the young girl; lines 21 to 24 narrate her going

58.reading: The man tells the girl, long-haired, deer-eyed, with a body like sprouts that meet the rains and a waist like a creeper, who swings her bangled arms and passes after taking his life, that because of her youth she does not know the sickness she causes and is not at fault, and her people will say they are not at fault for dressing her and sending her out in their wealth; so if he punishes anyone it will be her people, and if the sickness grows past bearing he will mount the palm-stem horse in the town square and fix the blame on her.
58.nuance: The madal threat here is aimed not at winning her but at blame: riding it will make the town see her as the cause (நீ படு பழியே). The three refrains rotate the reason her people dressed her (wealth, possession, riches), so the family's display is the real culprit.

thinai_evidence.note: one-sided love for a girl too young to know it, with the threat of madal

comparisons.tenor: her gaze like a doe's
her body like sprouts meeting the rains
her waist like a creeper

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man addresses the passing girl and threatens madal

59.reading: The man tells the girl who plays with toy pots and dolls, her bangles like lotus shoots and her forearm like the kaanthal's spathe, who passed leaving him without himself, that when the neighbours blame her as merciless to the one who suffers, the merit of her bathing in Thai among her friends, of the gifts she gave playing the little mother in others' houses, and of feeding her doll-baby and laughing with her friends will not help her; if she does not do what he asks, the fruit of her deeds will not let go, and there is nothing for those who desire once kindness lets go.
59.nuance: Each refrain sets a girl's ritual or play (the Thai bath, playing house, feeding the doll) against the neighbours' charge that she has no pity, so her childhood merit is weighed against a grown man's claim. Line 11 reads பழிக்கும்கா where the parallel lines 15 and 19 have பழிக்கும்கால்.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl still at play addressed by a man in love

comparisons.vehicle: தாமரை முளை நிமிர்ந்தவை போலும் முத்துக் கோல் அவிர் தொடி
comparisons.tenor: her pearl bangles like rising lotus shoots

comparisons.vehicle: காந்தள் நுண் ஏர் தண் ஏர் உருவின் துடுப்பு எனப் புரையும் நின் திரண்ட, நேர் அரி முன்கை
comparisons.tenor: her forearm like the kaanthal's spathe

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man addresses the girl at play

60.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who said it is unwomanly to give life-draining pain to those who glimpse such beauty bowed with tears and trembled, wasting like a fighting tusker, and asked the friend for the cure of the sickness her friend's eyes gave him, saying the only medicine is to see her face; what shall they do, she asks, and answers that though they once thought trusting a stranger in the street easy, it is not kind to send away with shame a man who gazes unblinking and longs for their friendship.
60.nuance: The friend reports the hero's plea as evidence and then turns it on the girl, ending in the persuasion that she accept him. Several phrases are obscure (வாரணவாசிப் பதம் பெயர்த்தல், line 13; பொன் செய்வாம், line 23), and lines 15 to 32 are not in sangamtamil.com's text.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend urges the girl to accept the suitor in kalavu

comparisons.tenor: her dark hair falling like rain
the man, a fighting tusker in bearing, wasting

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports the man's plea and urges the girl to accept him

61.reading: The friend, telling the girl of the man who keeps looking at her like a ruined noble who comes to kin but cannot say his need, asks him what he lacks, since the girl, whose father gives prized wealth to all and who holds that living without giving to suppliants is worse than death, would give it; he answers that he wants no wealth, only that her deer-eyed friend show him grace; she laughs that a man like a battle-winning tusker should lie waiting on a woman's grace and is shameless, yet he goes saying he will ride the mocked palm-stem horse if refused, comes back however they laugh, and will not leave without what he came for, so they must act before her father's heart is wounded.
61.nuance: The friend first treats him as a suppliant and offers the household's giving ethic, the puram creed that dying is sweeter than being unable to give; his answer moves the suppliant's role from wealth to love, which the giving household cannot refuse on its own terms.

thinai_evidence.note: the suitor asks the friend's help and threatens madal in kalavu

comparisons.tenor: his silent looks like a ruined noble unable to state his need to kin
he follows like a shadow that does not leave
the man like a tusker that has won in battle
his sidelong looks like a thief's

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend recounts her exchange with the suitor and urges the girl to yield

62.reading: The girl, speaking of a shameless man who takes the hand even of those who refuse him, reports how he said he embraced her because embracing her was sweet, how she asked whether it is right to force on others what pains them because it is sweet to oneself, and how he answered that people drink water because it is sweet to the thirsty, not to the water, and that he holds seizing moon-faced women to be virtue; if virtue too sees it so, she tells her heart, he will not hear reason and will torment her, and since they once said they were not two, what quarrel has her heart with him?
62.nuance: The exchange is a moral debate in miniature: she states the rule against doing to others what is sweet to oneself and painful to them, and he answers with a theory of pleasure (sweetness lies in the one who needs) and calls the seizing virtue; she gives way not to his argument but to their former bond. The speaker of line 12 to 13 (caught between the five-mouthed snake) may be either.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's embrace in kalavu and her consent

comparisons.tenor: the girl like a creeper with tender clusters

comparisons.vehicle: நீர்க்கு இனிது என்று உண்பவோ, நீர் உண்பவர்
comparisons.tenor: his desire like the thirsty drinking water, sweet to the drinker not the water
the girl caught by him like the moon seized by the five-mouthed snake
women whose faces shine like the spotless moon

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl recounts the dialogue and closes by addressing her heart

63.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man stares and bows to her careless of onlookers, and when she waves him off for fear of gossip he only waits to come again, so the place can no longer be guarded; she proposes that the girl not go to him herself, while she calls him as if she wanted him and then goes off to have sugarcane painted on her shoulder, telling her to ask him 'were you here?' and pass, for he will fall at her feet as the cure for his sickness; and, speaking to him, she makes him swear not to say the girl consented, and tells her that standing with him will be as easy as standing with her friend.
63.nuance: The friend stages a tryst made to look accidental, with herself as the caller and an errand (the sugarcane painting) as her excuse to leave, so that the girl's consent can be denied. The voices change without notice (lines 12 and 13 seem addressed to the man), so who says which part is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend arranges the lovers' meeting in kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the girl as the medicine for his sickness

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend plans the meeting with the girl, turning once to the man (lines 12 and 13)

64.reading: The man tells the woman, whose face is like the moon and whose dark hair, wound with alari flowers, is like the aaral fish, that she owes him a great sum of gold from long ago; the friend asks what gold they owe for the painting on her shoulder, since they have ploughed nothing, and he answers that the sugarcane drawn on her shoulders and the blue lily blooming like her face are her ploughing; the friend replies that he claims gold for her eyes too, and tells the girl that he would come at once if paid, as kings take tribute, but otherwise she should embrace him once in pretence and so cast off the whole debt.
64.nuance: The whole poem is a mock lawsuit: love is a debt of gold, the breast-painting is ploughed land, and an embrace pays it off. Several turns (lines 24 and 25, the closing உத்தி எறிந்துவிடற்கு) are obscure and the assignment of speakers is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's playful suit for an embrace in kalavu

comparisons.tenor: her face like the moon
her braid like the dark cloud
the flower-wound braid like the aaral fish
the blue lily blooming like her face
her eyes like a sharp iron blade
his claims like the tribute a king takes
the breast-painting as her ploughing

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: a dialogue in which the friend (addressed as இகுளை) answers for the girl

65.reading: The girl tells her friend of the night's farce, a joke for the whole town: as she waited wrapped in a fine cloth at her lover's tryst, the old crippled brahmin of their street, shaven-headed in a stained blanket, saw her, asked who stood there out of time, edged up like an old bull to straw, offered her betel from his pouch, and when she stood silent backed off crying that he was a goblin who would take the town's offerings; seeing him afraid, she threw a handful of sand on him and he raised a cry, so that like a stray little jackal caught in a net set for a fierce tiger, the old man spoiled her lover's coming and made an uproar for the town.
65.nuance: The comedy inverts the night tryst's dangers: the threat is no beast or guard but a frightened old man who mistakes her for a ghost and is mistaken by her for one in turn. The closing simile makes the brahmin the jackal and leaves the tiger the net was set for unnamed: the lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the night tryst of kalavu and its hindrance

comparisons.tenor: the old brahmin edging close like an old bull that has seen straw

comparisons.vehicle: இரும் புலி கொண்மார் நிறுத்த வலையுள் ஓர் ஏதில் குறு நரி பட்டற்றால்
comparisons.tenor: the brahmin caught in the tryst like a stray jackal in a net set for a tiger

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the girl tells her friend how the night tryst was spoiled

links.note: Purananuru 165 opens with those who wished to last in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து மன்னுதல் குறித்தோர்) and set up their fame; Kalittokai 54 ends with the girl wanting it said she acted from love, which in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து) is what lasts.
links.teaches: The akam heroine takes over the puram formula for lasting fame and applies it to a woman's choice of lover, so the Sangam ideal of a name that outlives one could be earned by love as well as by giving.

links.note: Kural 1117 asks whether a woman's face has spots as the moon does; Kalittokai 55 has the man make the same correction six times over (not the moon, for it has no stain; not the crescent, for it does not wane), reported by the girl.
links.teaches: The Kural's single corrected simile is shown in the Kalittokai as a wooing technique that the girl sees through, so the man's praise-by-correction is not only admiration but a calculated approach she names as such.

links.note: In Kural 1081 the man, first seeing her, cannot tell if she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Kalittokai 56 he asks if she is a craftsman's doll, a woman assembled from all women's best parts, or Death in a form it chose.
links.teaches: Both stage the first sight as a failure to classify the woman, but the Kalittokai adds Death and a girl too young to know her effect, so the Kural's bewilderment turns into a complaint that her beauty is a public danger no one has announced.

links.note: Kuruntokai 32 says appearing in the street on the palm-stem horse is blame (பழியே) for the man; Kalittokai 58 has the man say riding it will fix the blame on the girl (நீ படு பழியே).
links.teaches: On a defensible reading the two disagree about whom the madal shames, the rider or the woman, which shows the threat worked as leverage precisely because the disgrace could be made to fall on her household.

links.note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
links.teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

links.note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palm-stem horse; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the tusker-like warrior who threatens the mocked madal is truly without shame (நாண் இலன்).
links.teaches: The Kural gives the man's own confession that madal means the loss of shame and manliness; the Kalittokai gives the woman's side seeing that loss, and shows it is what persuades her that he will not stop.

links.note: Purananuru 12 asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma to take others' land so that it is painful to them (இன்னா ஆகப் பிறர் மண் கொண்டு) and do sweet things for his admirers; in Kalittokai 62 the girl asks whether forcing on others what pains them because it is sweet to oneself (தமக்கு இனிது என்று, வலிதின் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்வது) is good.
links.teaches: The same sweet-for-oneself, painful-for-others test is put to a conquering king and to a forceful lover, and in both the one questioned claims it as virtue (அறன்), so the Sangam poets judged seizure in war and in love by one moral rule.

links.note: Kural 316 says one must not do to another what one knows to be painful; in Kalittokai 62 the girl states that rule and the man answers that sweetness lies in the one who needs, and that seizing moon-faced women is virtue.
links.teaches: The Kalittokai lets the lover contest the Kural's rule with an argument from pleasure rather than ignore it, showing that the love poets knew the non-harm maxim and staged its failure under desire.

links.note: Kural 1102 says the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Kalittokai 60 the man tells the friend his only medicine is to see the girl's face, and there is no other.
links.teaches: The Kural states the paradox as the man's private discovery after union; in the Kalittokai it is relayed by the friend as a plea before union, so the same conceit serves as an argument that obliges the girl to grant the cure.

links.note: In Kalittokai 58 the man threatens madal to the girl herself; in 61 the friend reports the same threat, laughs at it as shameless, and still concludes they must act.
links.teaches: Read together they show where the madal threat lands: the girl too young to understand it in 58 cannot be moved by it, while the friend in 61 is, so the threat is effectively addressed to the household's guardians.

Line 11 reads பழிக்கும்கா where the parallel lines 15 and 19 read பழிக்கும்கால்; probably a dropped final ல்.
Lines 15 to 21 and 24 to 32 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; line 13 வாரணவாசிப் பதம் பெயர்த்தல் and line 23 பொன் செய்வாம் are obscure.
The colophon gives no thurai for any poem of this chapter; thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
